text: Somewhere tonight, a software engineer in
Bengaluru is sending another application to a
company in Berlin.
She doesn't know it yet, but that job was
never open to her.
Job boards are built for volume.
Search, click, apply, repeat.
But when you're applying across borders,
volume is the problem.
A listing may need a work permit you don't
have. The company may never sponsor a visa.
And none of that shows up in the match score.
So people apply everywhere, hear nothing back,
and slowly burn their name with recruiters.
That isn't a skills problem.
It's an information problem.
So we built Skylark.
A job application service that puts you
forward only for roles you can actually take,
explains every decision, and keeps a human in
the loop before anything is sent.
It starts with one profile.
Upload your resume, and Skylark pulls out your
headline, skills and experience.
Every field is checked on the server.
Skills, against a curated taxonomy,
Stack Overflow tags and the European ESCO
catalogue. Even your email domain is verified.
Your dashboard shows new matches,
active applications and today's progress.
Open any role, and you see exactly why it
fits. Seven factors, each with a score and a
sentence you can read.
When you decide to apply, AI drafts a tailored
resume and cover letter.
Every change comes with a reason,
and nothing is applied until you accept it.
Then a specialist takes over.
They work through a five-point checklist,
submit the application, and record the
employer's confirmation reference.
You follow every step on your tracker,
from saved, to applied, to interview.
Under the surface, Skylark is a pipeline.
Listings arrive from public job APIs:
Arbeitnow, sixteen Greenhouse company boards,
and others when they're configured.
Each posting is cleaned from raw HTML into a
title, seniority, location, salary,
sponsorship and skills.
An SHA-256 fingerprint collapses duplicates.
Stale listings are closed, and if nothing has
refreshed in twenty-four hours,
candidates are told.
Then the match engine scores every role
against your profile.
Skills carry thirty percent.
Eligibility, twenty.
Experience, eighteen.
Location, twelve.
Sponsorship, eight.
Preferences, seven.
And education, five.
The score is simply their weighted sum.
Now, here's the rule that matters most.
If a role won't sponsor someone who needs it,
the score is capped at thirty-five.
However strong your skills look,
a job you can't legally take will never
outrank one you can.
The product itself is one Next.js application:
the public website, the candidate app,
an operations console and a shared inbox.
Every service talks to a single repository
interface. In production, that's Supabase
Postgres, with row level security on every table.
Without credentials, the same interface runs
on a seeded in-memory store.
So the whole product works on a laptop,
with zero setup.
Security isn't assumed.
It's tested. The test suite applies every
migration to a real Postgres engine,
and proves that one candidate can never read
another's data.
AI sits behind an interface too.
Claude drafts the tailoring, and its output is
validated against a schema.
If the model is unavailable, a deterministic
rules engine takes over.
Background work runs through a queue.
Every task carries an idempotency key,
no two workers claim the same job,
and failures back off before they're set aside.
Today, Skylark is live at skylarkgo.in.
Live job listings.
Google sign-in. Chat-style onboarding.
Subscriptions in rupees through Razorpay.
And a specialist review queue with a
twenty-four hour target.
Next, we're adding more job sources for India,
and matching every candidate against the
entire catalogue.
Skylark doesn't try to send more applications.
It tries to send the right ones,
and to show you why.
Fewer applications.
Better reasons. And a person checking every one.
Skylark. Your next move, already in motion.
